title: Unit 731
description: Japanese biological and chemical warfare unit (1936–1945)
wiki_lead:
Unit 731 (731部隊, Nana-san-ichi Butai) was a secret biological and chemical warfare research unit run by the Imperial Japanese Army between 1933 and 1945. Officially known as the Manchu Detachment 731, it was also referred to as the Kamo Detachment and the Ishii Unit.
The main facility was based in the Pingfang district of Harbin, located within the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo (which is now Northeast China). From there, the unit managed multiple branches across mainland China and Southeast Asia under the "Epidemic Prevention Department" umbrella. During the Second Sino-Japanese War, the unit launched the largest biological weapons attacks in history. They killed an estimated 200,000 people in various cities and villages by intentionally poisoning water supplies, food, and crops.
The unit was led by General Shirō Ishii and received strong support from the Japanese military. An estimated 14,000 people were killed by human experimentation in the facility itself. Its activities included infecting prisoners with deadly diseases, conducting vivisection, performing organ harvesting, testing hypobaric chambers, amputating limbs, and exposing victims to chemical agents and explosives. Prisoners—often referred to as "logs" (or "maruta") by the staff—were mainly Chinese civilians, but also included Russians, Koreans, and others, including children and pregnant women. No documented survivors are currently known.
After the war, twelve Unit 731 members were tried by the USSR in the 1949 Khabarovsk war crimes trials and received relatively lenient prison sentences. However, Ishii and other Unit 731 personnel escaped prosecution by the United States because of U.S. concerns that a war crime trial would expose the data to the USSR and force the U.S. to publicly reveal their own biological warfare capabilities. Consequently, the Americans granted them immunity in exchange for their research data, despite knowing beforehand that the information was of no significant value to the United States. After reviewing the research, American scientists characterized Japanese weaponry as crude, while acknowledging that it was the first study to document human subjects. The Truman administration concealed the unit's crimes and paid stipends to former personnel.
On 28 August 2002, the Tokyo District Court acknowledged that Japan had conducted biological warfare in China and held the state responsible for related deaths, but rejected compensation, arguing this was provided by postwar treaties such as the Treaty of San Francisco. In April 2018, the National Archives of Japan released a near-complete list of 3,607 personnel affiliated with Unit 731. The Japanese government has never issued an official acknowledgement of its biological warfare. However, in the postwar period, former Unit 731 personnel published and shared their findings from human experiments, reflecting awareness and acceptance of these experiments within Japan’s medical community.

Directed by Lieutenant General ShirÅ Ishii, a microbiologist and army surgeon, the unit systematically subjected thousands of human prisonersâprimarily Chinese civilians and combatants, but also Soviet, Korean, and Allied personnelâto fatal experiments including live vivisections without anesthesia, deliberate infections with pathogens such as plague, anthrax, and cholera, pressure chamber tests causing explosive decompression, frostbite inductions followed by amputations, and exposure to biological and chemical weapons. These activities, disguised under the euphemism of the " Epidemic Prevention and Water Purification Department of the Kwantung Army," aimed to develop offensive biological agents for battlefield use, with field trials including aerial dispersal of plague-infected fleas over Chinese cities, resulting in widespread civilian deaths from engineered epidemics. At war's end, Unit 731 personnel demolished their facilities and records to conceal evidence, but Ishii and key scientists negotiated immunity from prosecution at the Tokyo Trials by surrendering extensive data to U.S. authorities, who prioritized the intelligence value over justice, integrating findings into American bioweapons programs while enforcing a cover-up that persisted for decades. The unit's operations exemplify state-sanctioned medical atrocities driven by wartime imperatives, with victim counts exceeding 3,000 directly in laboratories and potentially hundreds of thousands from deployed agents, underscoring failures in international oversight of dual-use scientific research.
